title: Juniper and the Well
premise: Folklorist Lior Oyelaran has spent two decades in the village of Hollowmere documenting songs no one will sing twice, telling themselves the house's noises have rational explanations. When every mirror begins reflecting one second late, Lior realizes the 'count' their late grandmother's lullaby describes is real: each frost pattern on the windows marks a soul the well below the house will claim, and it has begun counting Lior's found family—the foster kids and strays they've quietly sheltered for years. As the village elders, who have fed the well outsiders for generations, close ranks, Lior must choose between the anonymity that kept them safe and a public reckoning that could destroy everyone. In the end, Lior gives the well what it truly wants—not lives, but the truth of its last victim's name, sung aloud at last—and carries the family out ahead of the final frost, leaving Hollowmere to face its own reflection.
about_author: Z. M. Blackwood is the pen name of a former archivist of regional folk music who spent years collecting songs in remote villages before turning to fiction. They write horror about quiet places, inherited debts, and the families we build when our blood relations fail us.

chapters.title: The Song Nobody Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Recording an elderly singer who stops mid-verse, pale, refusing to continue a lullaby about a counting frost. Lior notices the singer glanced at the window as if expecting something. Establishes Lior's methodical skepticism and their warm but guarded household of strays. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. At home, Lior catches their own reflection lagging—a blink arriving after the blink. They test every mirror with a metronome; all reflect one second behind. The youngest foster kid, Tam, admits he's seen 'the slow me' for weeks but thought Lior would be angry. Emotional beat: the collapse of twenty years of rational explanations.

chapters.title: The Household
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. A tender portrait of the found family: three foster kids, a disgraced nurse named Odile, and old Mr. Fenn who repairs clocks. Tam maps the house's noises—footsteps upstairs when no one is up there, water running in a dry bathroom. He loves this fragile home fiercely. Emotional beat: love sharpening into dread as he realizes the house is listening back.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Notebook
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Searching the attic, Lior finds their grandmother's folklore notebook: the same lullaby, transcribed, with marginalia—'the well counts by frost,' 'it takes the unnamed first.' A pressed photograph shows villagers, faces scratched out, standing around the wellhead. Emotional beat: grief curdling into betrayal as Lior realizes family knew.

chapters.title: The First Pattern
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Frost ferns bloom across the kitchen window overnight—in July. Odile, pragmatic, counts the branches: seven. There are six people in the house. She says nothing, starts packing go-bags in secret, and lies smoothly at breakfast. Emotional beat: protective denial, the price of keeping calm for the children.

chapters.title: Village Hospitality
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior brings the notebook question to the village archive and meets stonewalling wrapped in kindness: tea, deflection, a warning from the archivist, Mrs. Aldery, to 'let sleeping verses lie.' Outside, someone has chalked a tally mark on Lior's gatepost. Emotional beat: the realization that invisibility was always granted, never owned.

chapters.title: What Tam Heard Downstairs
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Waking at 3 a.m., Tam hears the dry bathroom running and, beneath the floor, a wet rhythmic sound like swallowing. He follows it to the cellar hatch, locked from outside with a new padlock that wasn't there yesterday. Someone in the house—or something wearing someone—is feeding below. Emotional beat: childhood ending in a single cold hallway.

chapters.title: The Second Pattern
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A second frost pattern appears, and this time the count is wrong: eight branches, six people. Unless the well counts the dead grandmother too—or is counting ahead. Lior cross-references the lullaby's verses with past disappearances in parish records: every nineteen years, names vanish, always 'newcomers.' Emotional beat: horror becoming arithmetic.

chapters.title: Mr. Fenn's Confession
chapters.summary: Mr. Fenn's POV. The clockmaker admits he came to Hollowmere fleeing his own guilt and knew about the well from the start; he chose this house because being near it meant being left alone. He teaches them the rule he's survived by: never be counted, never be named aloud indoors. Emotional beat: shame offered as inheritance, refused as excuse.

chapters.title: Unnaming
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The household attempts Fenn's protocol: no names spoken inside, mirrors covered, a week of hushed routines that frays the children badly. Teenager Sef rebels, shouting her own name into the cellar hatch—'Come and take it then!' That night, a third frost pattern blooms. Emotional beat: the cost of silence measured in a child's anger.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldery's Ledger
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Breaking into the village archive at night, Lior finds Aldery's ledger: generations of 'offerings'—vagrants, travelers, unwanted babies—fed to the well to spare the founding families. Lior's own grandmother's name appears not as victim but as keeper. Emotional beat: justice and nausea intertwined; the law here was always the well.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Mark
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Confronting Aldery, Lior learns the role of keeper passes by blood and that Lior, as the last Oyelaran, was always meant to inherit: choose the offerings, keep the count, stay invisible. Aldery offers a bargain—name your strangers, keep your children. Emotional beat: temptation framed as mercy, recognized as rot.

chapters.title: Sef Is Counted
chapters.summary: Sef's POV. After the rebellion, Sef begins hearing the lullaby hummed in her own voice from empty rooms. Her reflection starts lagging further behind—two seconds, three—until it moves independently, smiling when she doesn't. She hides it, ashamed, then finally tells Tam. Emotional beat: terror shared halved, but time visibly running out.

chapters.title: The Well Itself
chapters.summary: Lior and Odile's alternating POV. They open the cellar hatch together and descend: the 'well' is older than the house, a stone throat ringed with scratched names, the newest scratches still wet. Voices rise from it singing the lullaby in every voice ever taken—including, briefly, Lior's mother's. Emotional beat: awe and violation; the archive of the erased.

chapters.title: Running Ahead of the Frost
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. The household flees at night through frozen fields though it's midsummer; frost follows them along hedgerows like a tide line. Fenn's truck dies two miles out. In the rearview mirror, the road behind reflects a house that is no longer there. Emotional beat: desperate hope discovering that the well does not respect distance.

chapters.title: What Follows
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Sheltering in a chapel ruin, they realize the frost patterns now appear on any glass near any of them, and the count has reached nine. Running spreads the well's reach instead of escaping it. Odile proposes the unthinkable: go back, end it at the source. Emotional beat: survival reframed—fleeing is also a way of paying forever.

chapters.title: The Nineteenth Year
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Research converges: the cycle peaks tonight, the nineteenth year, when the well must be 'satisfied' or it widens its count indefinitely. The lullaby's missing verse, recovered from the ledger, isn't a summons—it's a naming rite. The well cannot take what is truly named and mourned. Emotional beat: the weapon hidden inside the curse.

chapters.title: Aldery's Choice
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldery's POV. Returning to Hollowmere, they find the village preparing its own offering—a drifter trussed in the churchyard—to buy another nineteen years. Aldery, dying, hands Lior the keeper's iron key and asks, for once, to be forgiven rather than obeyed. Emotional beat: complicity meeting its limit; justice beginning outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: The Naming
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Climax. At the wellhead, Lior sings the full lullaby and speaks the name of the well's first victim—a child drowned by the founders, unnamed for two centuries—recovered from a baptismal fragment in the ledger. The well goes still. The frost patterns peel off the glass like skin. The villagers' reflections arrive one second early, showing what they'll become. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into reckoning.

chapters.title: What the Village Owes
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. No mob justice, no fire: instead Lior reads the ledger aloud in the churchyard, every offering's name restored, forcing Hollowmere to bury and mark real graves. Some villagers flee; some kneel; Aldery signs a confession before witnesses. The law failed for two hundred years, so memory becomes the sentence. Emotional beat: austere, unsentimental justice.

chapters.title: Six, Not Seven
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Back home, mirrors reflect on time. The seventh frost branch, they understand now, was never a person—it was the well itself, waiting to be let go. Tam unpacks the go-bags, keeps one packed by the door anyway, because some lessons stay. The household eats dinner loudly, saying each other's names over and over just because they can. Emotional beat: tenderness earned through terror.

chapters.title: Songs You Can Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, epilogue. One year later, Lior publishes the lullaby complete, credited to its true first singer, and records the village children singing it twice, laughing between takes. The cellar is sealed with light, not locks. On the last page of the new notebook, Lior writes: staying invisible was never living. Emotional beat: quiet, hard-won peace.
